title: Meeting for worship
hook: Quakers sit in silence until someone is moved to speak

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nickel Mines: a forgiveness that went to the gunman's family. Your line was forgiveness chose them. What did you decide ahead of time? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-five.

A plain room. Benches facing each other around the walls. No pulpit, no altar, nobody up front. People come in, sit down, and say nothing. Minutes pass. A cough. A bench creaks. A bird outside. Then a woman near the window stands, says a few sentences about something she's been carrying, and sits down again. Nobody answers her. The silence closes over her words like water. That's a Quaker meeting, at least in the kind Friends call unprogrammed. Quakers, the Religious Society of Friends, are today's room. Today's word is the name they give that hour: meeting for worship.

In an unprogrammed meeting there's no set order of service and no minister leading it. Friends gather in silence and wait on God together. That silence isn't empty, and it isn't a pause before the real thing starts. It is the real thing. Friends call it expectant waiting: waiting the way you'd wait at a station for someone you know is coming. Behind it stands a promise of Jesus: "For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." And a line from the psalms: "Be still, and know that I am God." When someone feels moved by the Spirit to speak, they stand and give what Friends call ministry. A few words, a verse, a memory, sometimes a song. Then they sit, and the silence returns. Nobody replies or argues. The words are left to settle. Robert Barclay, an early Quaker writer, described coming into these silent meetings and feeling a hidden power among the people that touched his heart, and as he gave way to it, the good in him was raised up. Friends still speak of a gathered meeting, when the whole room seems to go still together. When the hour is done, someone turns and shakes a neighbor's hand, and the handshakes spread around the room. Not every Quaker meeting looks like this. Programmed Friends churches have a pastor, hymns and a sermon, often with a time of open silence inside the service. Both are Quaker, and both make room to wait on God.

Here's the practice: a small meeting for worship. If someone's nearby, you can sit together; if not, sit alone. Let your breath slow and the room go quiet. Don't fill the silence with a to-do list. Wait, the way you'd wait for a friend at the station. If a thought rises that seems worth keeping, hold it, and let it sink back into the quiet. If you pray, you can wait on God. If you don't, simply wait and listen. Later today, if you can, try ten minutes. The bell holds the time.
Meeting for worship. The Quaker gathering in silence, waiting on God together, where anyone may be moved to speak.
Your line: expectant waiting. Today, in one gap, a line, a red light, a kettle, wait without reaching for your phone, and listen. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: In unprogrammed Quaker meetings, Friends gather in silence and wait on God; anyone moved to speak stands and offers a few words, and the meeting closes with handshakes. Programmed Friends churches have a pastor, hymns and a sermon, often with a time of open silence.

notes: Editor pass: 'both are waiting on the same God' (narrator theology) changed to 'both make room to wait on God'.
Unprogrammed and programmed Friends both described, without ranking or counts. Confirm wording ('no minister leading it'; programmed churches 'often with a time of open silence').
Barclay's account (Apology, Proposition 11, section 7: the 'secret power' in silent assemblies, the evil weakening and the good raised up) is paraphrased, not quoted; confirm the paraphrase.
Handshake to close the meeting and the term 'gathered meeting' are described as Friends' practice; confirm.
Bench arrangement in the hook ('facing each other around the walls') is illustrative; meetinghouses vary.
Outline practice is ten minutes of silence; the app's sit is two minutes, so ten minutes is offered as a later invitation.
